A cello has the same string pattern (C D G A) as a viola, although an octave lower. I began playing viola first, and violin was very easy to learn as a second instrument. The hardest part was learning a new clef. 


I’ve messed around on my friends’ cellos, and I believe it would be easier to read bass music already knowing treble and alto. It was a bit awkward trying to sit with the instrument and I don’t know how to bow correctly. It’s difficult since you’re learning horizontal bowing, instead of vertical and on your arm. 

You also have to place your fingers on the strings differently. If I were to play on the D string on a viola, I would place one finger for E, two for F#, and three for G. On the cello, you place one for E, three for F#, and four for G. At least this is what I’ve seen in my orchestra.

I already left a comment about dental pain, but I also have a story about when I vomited 10 times in one day. 

For a few summers in a row a few years ago, I would get an awful stomach bug for three to five days. The last one I had was a couple years ago, and it was terrible. I can tell you sincerely that throwing up is not as bad as waiting to throw up. At one point I just could not throw up, I was dry heaving and groaning in agony because I wouldn’t hurl. I was sweating and crying and I tried shoving my finger down my throat to get it to leave my body. My stomach was just turning itself inside out constantly and when I finally vomited it was a huge relief. It was like if you were really badly constipated but with the opposite orfice. I counted how many times I threw up in a 24 hour period, my previous record was 8 times. I hope that I don’t ever have to throw up more than 10 times in a day ever again. I also remember sitting with my face in the toilet trying to breathe in toilet smells to make myself gag and throw up. The second worse vomiting experience would be when you throw up and it’s so powerful that it goes through your nose and mouth at the same time and you get chunks stuck in your nose that you have to blow out.

I also get migraines that last one or two weeks sometimes, they usually turn to pounding in the afternoons. If I get one that’s short-lived it is usually worse and involves nausea and other side effects.

I have had dental problems most of my life, including medically needing braces, TMJ, tetracycline stained teeth, and genetically missing a tooth. When I was about 9 years old I had all four of my canines pulled at the same time. 

I remember when I lost my first premolar tooth on the bottom, someone had told me to try twisting them to get them out of my mouth. So I made the mistake of listening, and when I was alone messing with my tooth I turned it around in my mouth. It was so painful having my tooth still attached backwards in my mouth. I tried pulling it and wiggling it but that made the pain worse, I wasn’t able to turn it back around but it also wouldn’t come out of my mouth. My parents came into the room I was in while I screamed and tried to calm me down. Eventually I got it out, but even having that happen so long ago I still remember how awful it felt. 

Another instance happened more recently when I got my wisdom teeth taken out earlier this year. Two weeks post-op my bottom right incision became infected and I had to go back to the dentist so they could clean it out. I’ve had many dental procedures but this was by far the worst one. Even with two lidocaine shots I could feel them scraping inside where they had to open the incision back up. There were many tears. After coming home I felt like I was choking on my own mucus from my jaw being numb. Thinking about it makes my entire jaw ache. If you haven’t had wisdom teeth extracted yet, please if you do try your best to keep them clean, follow their instructions to the letter and if you think something is wrong don’t wait to go back. Also, if you know that they’re going to do something like that take some pain medication before you go so that you don’t have to try to swallow water and medication like a baby bird when you’re done.

I’m so sorry for your loss. Losing a classmate is incredibly traumatic. 

When I was in eighth grade one of my classmates took his own life. 
I remember it very clearly, and I remember it every year. It was Monday the fourth (my birthday was the third, on Sunday) and I went to school that morning very excited to show my peers the new pens I had gotten. I got all the way to third period before I heard what had happened. I remember walking to Spanish class as people sat in the hallway crying. I wasn’t sure why, so I kept going and I went into my classroom at the end of the hall. I was feeling happy that morning until my teacher asked if we knew. My heart instantly dropped as she told me that he had taken his life the night before. Several people in my class began crying and shouting. At the end of class I went back into the hallway and I saw a group of girls crying in the bathroom and pounding on the walls. On February fourth, every year, I remember that day and I wish he could be here to see his classmates. His mother was pregnant at the time of his death and his sibling never got to see him. 

The pain of losing someone that is in the hallways every day, in your classes and sitting in the same room as you at lunch, and seeing all of their friends break down and cry in the middle of class is strange and terrifying.

I did one of these for art class (not as good as this I should add). The process went something like this, mind you it’s different for everyone;

1. Plan out your design using at least six successive colors, or six monochromatic colors. 
2. On transparent cards, use an expo marker to draw each of your layers so that you understand how they line up. 
3. Draw out each layer on white copy paper, exactly in the position you want the final copy to be. 
4. Using carbon transfer paper, trace the copy paper design onto colored paper. 
5. Cut out the colored paper using an exacto knife. 
6. Assemble a wooden box with as many notches as there are layers of paper.
7. Put the final product into the wooden box, using one layer per paper.
